items.readable_text:
Content:
Some sequences are defined recursively, which means that there is a formula to get from one term to the next.

Content:
For example, suppose that we have the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n+1}=a_n+{\color{blue}{2}}, \quad a_1 = {\color{red}{3}}]

Content:
In this formula,

Content:
- the statement [MATH: a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{blue}{2}}] means "to get to the next term, we add [MATH: {\color{blue}{2}}] to the previous term," and
- the statement [MATH: a_1 = {\color{red}{3}}] tells us that the first term is [MATH: {\color{red}{3}}.]

Content:
So how do we calculate [MATH: a_2], the next term in the sequence? Easy! We plug [MATH: n=1] into the formula:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n + 1}|= a_{n} + 2; a_{1 + 1}|= a_{1} + 2; a_{2}|= a_{1} + 2; a_{2}|= 3 + 2; a_{2}|= 5]

Content:
Now that we know [MATH: a_2,] we can find [MATH: a_3] by plugging in [MATH: n=2] into the formula:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n + 1}|= a_{n} + 2; a_{2 + 1}|= a_{2} + 2; a_{3}|= a_{2} + 2; a_{3}|= 5 + 2; a_{3}|= 7]

Content:
We can keep going by substituting [MATH: n=3,4,5,] and so on. The resulting terms of the sequence are as follows:
[MATH: 3,\qquad 5,\qquad 7,\qquad 9,\qquad 11,\ldots]

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: a_{n+1}=2a_n-3] with [MATH: a_1=4,] then find the value of [MATH: a_2.]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: a_{n+1}=2a_n-3] with [MATH: a_1=4,] then find the value of [MATH: a_2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The recursive formula is [MATH: a_{n+1}=2a_n - 3] where [MATH: a_1={\color{blue}4}.]

We compute [MATH: a_2] by substituting [MATH: n=1] into the recursive formula:

[MATH: a_{n + 1}|= 2a_{n} − 3; a_{1 + 1}|= 2a_{1} − 3; a_{2}|= 2a_{1} − 3; a_{2}|= 2(4) − 3; a_{2}|= 5]

Therefore, [MATH: a_2=5.]

  • To compute [MATH: f(3),] we substitute [MATH: n=2] into the recursive formula: [MATH: f(n + 1)|= 2f(n) + 1; f(2 + 1)|= 2f(2) + 1; f(3)|= 2f(2) + 1; f(3)|= 2(7) + 1; f(3)|= 15]

  • To compute [MATH: f(4),] we substitute [MATH: n=3] into the recursive formula: [MATH: f(n + 1)|= 2f(n) + 1; f(3 + 1)|= 2f(3) + 1; f(4)|= 2f(3) + 1; f(4)|= 2(15) + 1; f(4)|= 31]

Therefore, the fourth term of the sequence is [MATH: f(4) = 31.]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the following sequence: [MATH: 1, \quad 6, \quad 11, \quad 16, \quad 21, \quad 26, \quad \dots] The recursive formula for this sequence is given by [MATH: f(n+1) = f(n) + \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,, \qquad f(1) = \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,.] From left to right, what are the missing values?
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following sequence:
[MATH: 1, \quad 6, \quad 11, \quad 16, \quad 21, \quad 26, \quad \dots]
The recursive formula for this sequence is given by
[MATH: f(n+1) = f(n) + \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,, \qquad f(1) = \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,.]
From left to right, what are the missing values?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the first term of the sequence is [MATH: f(1) = {\color{blue}1}.]

Inspecting the terms of the sequence, we see that we always get the next term by adding [MATH: {\color{red}5}.]

Therefore, the recursive rule must be the following: [MATH: f(n+1) = f(n) + \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{{\color{red}5}}\,, \qquad f(1) = \bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{{\color{blue}1}}]

So, the missing values are [MATH: 5] and [MATH: 1.]
